lessons.name: Analyze passages from To Kill a Mockingbird : Part 2

content.text: Read the following passage from To Kill a Mockingbird. In this excerpt, a violent mob arrives at the town jail to kill Tom Robinson, an African American man who has been accused of assaulting a white woman. Tom's lawyer, Atticus Finch, stands in the mob's way. Scout, Atticus's daughter and the novel's narrator, watches nearby as the scene begins.

textContent.text: "He in there, Mr. Finch?" a man said.
"He is," we heard Atticus answer, "and he's asleep. Don't wake him up."
"You know what we want," another man said. "Get aside from the door, Mr. Finch."
I pushed my way through dark smelly bodies and burst into the circle of light. "H-ey, Atticus!"

I thought he would have a fine surprise, but his face killed my joy. A flash of plain fear was going out of his eyes, […] and when I glanced around I discovered that these men were strangers. […] I sought once more for a familiar face, and at the center of the semi-circle I found one.
"Hey, Mr. Cunningham."
The man did not hear me, it seemed.
"Hey, Mr. Cunningham. How's your entailment¹ gettin' along?"

Mr. Walter Cunningham's legal affairs were well known to me; Atticus had once described them at length. The big man blinked and hooked his thumbs in his overall straps. He seemed uncomfortable; he cleared his throat and looked away. My friendly overture had fallen flat. […] He shifted his feet, clad in heavy work shoes.

"Don't you remember me, Mr. Cunningham? I'm Jean Louise Finch. You brought us some hickory nuts one time, remember?" I began to sense the futility one feels when unacknowledged by a chance acquaintance.
"I go to school with Walter," I began again. "He's your boy, ain't he? Ain't he, sir?"
Mr. Cunningham was moved to a faint nod. He did know me, after all.

"He's in my grade," I said, "and he does right well. He's a good boy," I added, "a real nice boy. We brought him home for dinner one time. Maybe he told you about me, I beat him up one time but he was real nice about it. Tell him hey for me, won't you?"

Atticus had said it was the polite thing to talk to people about what they were interested in, not about what you were interested in. Mr. Cunningham displayed no interest in his son, so I tackled his entailment once more in a last-ditch effort to make him feel at home.

"Entailments are bad," I was advising him, when I slowly awoke to the fact that I was addressing the entire aggregation. The men were all looking at me, some had their mouths half-open. […] Their attention amounted to fascination. Atticus's mouth, even, was half-open, an attitude he had once described as uncouth. Our eyes met and he shut it.

"Well, Atticus, I was just sayin' to Mr. Cunningham that entailments are bad an' all that, but you said not to worry, it takes a long time sometimes…that you all'd ride it out together…" I was slowly drying up, wondering what idiocy I had committed. Entailments seemed all right enough for livingroom talk.
I began to feel sweat gathering at the edges of my hair; I could stand anything but a bunch of people looking at me. They were quite still.
"What's the matter?" I asked.

Atticus said nothing. I looked around and up at Mr. Cunningham, whose face was equally impassive. Then he did a peculiar thing. He squatted down and took me by both shoulders. "I'll tell him you said hey, little lady," he said.
Then he straightened up and waved a big paw. "Let's clear out," he called. "Let's get going, boys."

<citation>From Harper Lee, To Kill a Mockingbird. Copyright 1960 by Harper Lee</citation>

content.text: No Place Like Home

alternativeText.text: There is a large mural on a wall outside. In the mural, a man sits under a lamp, and three children stand next to him. Some men come out of cars and gather around the man and children.

pieces.text: When director Robert Mulligan set out to turn

content.text: To Kill a Mockingbird

pieces.text: into a movie, he consulted the book's author, Harper Lee, to make sure he accurately preserved the story's details.

The film's art director was even sent to Lee's childhood hometown of Monroeville, Alabama, the inspiration for the novel's fictional setting of Maycomb. Lee accompanied the art director, who photographed and sketched porches, collard patches, and the courthouse, a setting that features prominently in the novel and film. She also provided the filmmaker with photographs of the town from the 1930s, when the story takes place.

content.text: The movie's artistic choices, including the use of black-and-white film and eerie sound effects, highlight the disturbing intersection of quaint small-town life with the dark realities of racism and poverty in the Jim Crow South.

pieces.text: Lee loved the novel's film adaptation and called it "one of the best translations of a book to film ever made."

content.text: Scout shows that she listens closely when her father discusses his clients' legal issues, but she does not have the experience or knowledge about the world to recognize the gravity or danger of the situation she enters.

While Scout does ask Mr. Cunningham many questions, she uses them primarily to engage him in friendly conversation, not to pry into his legal affairs. She tries to appeal to his interests to make him feel comfortable.

When Scout realizes that she has the attention of the entire group, she expresses discomfort with having "a bunch of people looking at" her. This suggests she is not putting on a show for the sake of attention.
Review the passage. Then, select two details that best suggest that Scout is persistent and bold.

content.text: When Mr. Cunningham does not respond to Scout's previous questions, she continues to try to capture his attention by asking about his son. She repeats the phrase "ain't he" in an effort to elicit a response.

Scout does not understand Mr. Cunningham's reluctance to acknowledge her and begins to feel a sense of rejection or inadequacy. The description of her feelings conveys her frustration with Mr. Cunningham's lack of response despite her repeated attempts.

pieces.text: When director Robert Mulligan set out to turn

content.text: To Kill a Mockingbird

pieces.text: into a movie, he consulted the book's author, Harper Lee, to make sure he accurately preserved the story's details.

The film's art director was even sent to Lee's childhood hometown of Monroeville, Alabama, the inspiration for the novel's fictional setting of Maycomb. Lee accompanied the art director, who photographed and sketched porches, collard patches, and the courthouse, a setting that features prominently in the novel and film. She also provided the filmmaker with photographs of the town from the 1930s, when the story takes place.

content.text: The movie's artistic choices, including the use of black-and-white film and eerie sound effects, highlight the disturbing intersection of quaint small-town life with the dark realities of racism and poverty in the Jim Crow South.

pieces.text: Lee loved the novel's film adaptation and called it "one of the best translations of a book to film ever made."

contents.text: The details in these two quotes suggest that Scout is persistent and bold:

text.text: "I go to school with Walter," I began again. "He's your boy, ain't he? Ain't he, sir?"

content.text: When Mr. Cunningham does not respond to Scout's previous questions, she continues to try to capture his attention by asking about his son. She repeats the phrase "ain't he" in an effort to elicit a response.

text.text: Mr. Cunningham displayed no interest in his son, so I tackled his entailment once more in a last-ditch effort to make him feel at home.

content.text: After another failed attempt to engage with Mr. Cunningham, Scout tries returning to the earlier topic of the man's entailment, even though it seems clear that he is trying to ignore her.
Look at the word in bold.

textContent.text: "He in there, Mr. Finch?" a man said.
"He is," we heard Atticus answer, "and he's asleep. Don't wake him up."
"You know what we want," another man said. "Get aside from the door, Mr. Finch."
I pushed my way through dark smelly bodies and burst into the circle of light. "H-ey, Atticus!"

I thought he would have a fine surprise, but his face killed my joy. A flash of plain fear was going out of his eyes, […] and when I glanced around I discovered that these men were strangers. […] I sought once more for a familiar face, and at the center of the semi-circle I found one.
"Hey, Mr. Cunningham."
The man did not hear me, it seemed.
"Hey, Mr. Cunningham. How's your entailment¹ gettin' along?"

Mr. Walter Cunningham's legal affairs were well known to me; Atticus had once described them at length. The big man blinked and hooked his thumbs in his overall straps. He seemed uncomfortable; he cleared his throat and looked away. My friendly overture had fallen flat. […] He shifted his feet, clad in heavy work shoes.

"Don't you remember me, Mr. Cunningham? I'm Jean Louise Finch. You brought us some hickory nuts one time, remember?" I began to sense the futility one feels when unacknowledged by a chance acquaintance.
"I go to school with Walter," I began again. "He's your boy, ain't he? Ain't he, sir?"
Mr. Cunningham was moved to a faint nod. He did know me, after all.

"He's in my grade," I said, "and he does right well. He's a good boy," I added, "a real nice boy. We brought him home for dinner one time. Maybe he told you about me, I beat him up one time but he was real nice about it. Tell him hey for me, won't you?"

Atticus had said it was the polite thing to talk to people about what they were interested in, not about what you were interested in. Mr. Cunningham displayed no interest in his son, so I tackled his entailment once more in a last-ditch effort to make him feel at home.

"Entailments are bad," I was advising him, when I slowly awoke to the fact that I was addressing the entire aggregation. The men were all looking at me, some had their mouths half-open. […] Their attention amounted to fascination. Atticus's mouth, even, was half-open, an attitude he had once described as uncouth. Our eyes met and he shut it.

"Well, Atticus, I was just sayin' to Mr. Cunningham that entailments are bad an' all that, but you said not to worry, it takes a long time sometimes…that you all'd ride it out together…" I was slowly drying up, wondering what idiocy I had committed. Entailments seemed all right enough for livingroom talk.
I began to feel sweat gathering at the edges of my hair; I could stand anything but a bunch of people looking at me. They were quite still.
"What's the matter?" I asked.

Atticus said nothing. I looked around and up at Mr. Cunningham, whose face was equally impassive. Then he did a peculiar thing. He squatted down and took me by both shoulders. "I'll tell him you said hey, little lady," he said.
Then he straightened up and waved a big paw. "Let's clear out," he called. "Let's get going, boys."

contents.text: The details in the passage suggest that this is how Scout's behavior changes the nature of the confrontation:

text.text: Her attempt at small talk makes the men reconsider their behavior and reduces the likelihood of violence.

content.text: Scout's attempts at casual conversation contrast immensely with the threatening dialogue at the beginning of the scene. Out of discomfort with her recognition of him, Mr. Cunningham initially ignores Scout. But eventually, her words seem to remind him of his family and his relationship with Atticus. Scout seems to make him feel more like an individual and less like a member of a mob.

contents.text: The details in the passage do not suggest the following:

text.text: Her deliberate shaming of Mr. Cunningham makes the men feel vulnerable and less sure of their abilities.

content.text: Scout's discussion of Mr. Cunningham's legal issues is not intended to shame him, but rather to "make him feel at home."

text.text: Her indifference to her father's authority causes the men to question Atticus's reputation in the community.

content.text: Scout's statements about entailments are based on what her father has told her about his client's legal affairs. The passage does not suggest that this discussion affects the other men's opinions about Atticus and his standing in the community.

text.text: Her surprising bravery and convincing argument inspire the men to reconsider their opinion of Tom Robinson.

content.text: Scout does not recognize the danger posed by the men, so she is not intentionally acting bravely. And while the men do decide to halt their violent plan, this does not seem to be due to a shift in their opinion of Tom Robinson.

Scout does not understand Mr. Cunningham's reluctance to acknowledge her and begins to feel a sense of rejection or inadequacy. The description of her feelings conveys her frustration with Mr. Cunningham's lack of response despite her repeated attempts.

pieces.text: When director Robert Mulligan set out to turn

content.text: To Kill a Mockingbird

pieces.text: into a movie, he consulted the book's author, Harper Lee, to make sure he accurately preserved the story's details.

The film's art director was even sent to Lee's childhood hometown of Monroeville, Alabama, the inspiration for the novel's fictional setting of Maycomb. Lee accompanied the art director, who photographed and sketched porches, collard patches, and the courthouse, a setting that features prominently in the novel and film. She also provided the filmmaker with photographs of the town from the 1930s, when the story takes place.

content.text: The movie's artistic choices, including the use of black-and-white film and eerie sound effects, highlight the disturbing intersection of quaint small-town life with the dark realities of racism and poverty in the Jim Crow South.

pieces.text: Lee loved the novel's film adaptation and called it "one of the best translations of a book to film ever made."

content.text: When Scout realizes that she has the attention of the entire group, she expresses discomfort with having "a bunch of people looking at" her. This suggests she is not putting on a show for the sake of attention.

Scout shows that she listens closely when her father discusses his clients' legal issues, but she does not have the experience or knowledge about the world to recognize the gravity or danger of the situation she enters.

content.text: Scout's attempts at casual conversation contrast immensely with the threatening dialogue at the beginning of the scene. Scout seems to make him feel more like an individual and less like a member of a mob.

text.text: Her indifference to her father's authority causes the men to question Atticus's reputation in the community.

content.text: Scout's statements about entailments are based on what her father has told her about his client's legal affairs. The passage does not suggest that this discussion affects the other men's opinions about Atticus and his standing in the community.

content.text: Scout does not recognize the danger posed by the men, so she is not intentionally acting bravely. And while the men do decide to halt their violent plan, this does not seem to be due to a shift in their opinion of Tom Robinson.

She recognizes Mr. Cunningham as her father's client and recalls him bringing hickory nuts to her family. However, when Scout tries to be friendly with Mr. Cunningham, he awkwardly ignores her attempts at small talk. She repeats words like "remember" and "ain't he" and tries several times to shift the topic and begin again, seemingly without effect.

Scout does not understand Mr. Cunningham's reluctance to acknowledge her and begins to feel a sense of rejection or inadequacy. The description of her feelings conveys her frustration with Mr. Cunningham's lack of response despite her repeated attempts.

alternativeText.text: There is a large mural on a wall outside. In the mural, a man sits under a lamp, and three children stand next to him. Some men come out of cars and gather around the man and children.

pieces.text: When director Robert Mulligan set out to turn

content.text: To Kill a Mockingbird

pieces.text: into a movie, he consulted the book's author, Harper Lee, to make sure he accurately preserved the story's details.

The film's art director was even sent to Lee's childhood hometown of Monroeville, Alabama, the inspiration for the novel's fictional setting of Maycomb. Lee accompanied the art director, who photographed and sketched porches, collard patches, and the courthouse, a setting that features prominently in the novel and film. She also provided the filmmaker with photographs of the town from the 1930s, when the story takes place.

content.text: The movie's artistic choices, including the use of black-and-white film and eerie sound effects, highlight the disturbing intersection of quaint small-town life with the dark realities of racism and poverty in the Jim Crow South.

pieces.text: Lee loved the novel's film adaptation and called it "one of the best translations of a book to film ever made."

content.text: Scout shows that she listens closely when her father discusses his clients' legal issues, but she does not have the experience or knowledge about the world to recognize the gravity or danger of the situation she enters.

When Scout realizes that she has the attention of the entire group, she expresses discomfort with having "a bunch of people looking at" her. This suggests she is not putting on a show for the sake of attention.

While Scout does ask Mr. Cunningham many questions, she uses them primarily to engage him in friendly conversation, not to pry into his legal affairs. She tries to appeal to his interests to make him feel comfortable.

contents.text: In argumentative writing, transitions can clarify the relationships between claims, evidence, analysis, counterclaims, and responses to counterclaims. Different transitions serve different purposes:

header.text: Connecting a claim to evidence that supports the claim

contents.text: Those who learn how to deal with setbacks when they are young often succeed later in life. Consider, for example, founding father Benjamin Franklin, who had to leave school at age ten due to a lack of money but continued learning on his own and became one of the most celebrated writers of his age.
Other transitions that show this type of relationship include for instance, to illustrate, and for example.

header.text: Connecting two pieces of supporting evidence

contents.text: Delaying the start of the school day to allow students to sleep later has a number of benefits. Additionally, a number of studies indicate that students whose schools switch to later start times experience lower rates of driving accidents and substance abuse.
Other transitions that show this type of relationship include furthermore, likewise, moreover, and in a similar vein.

header.text: Connecting supporting evidence to analysis of that evidence

contents.text: In our information-saturated world, people are losing the ability to sustain focus for extended periods of time. Blog posts of today are shorter, on average, than they were ten to fifteen years ago. Evidently, people are less willing than they once were to read long chunks of text.

contents.text: <instructions>Which of the following contains a vague pronoun reference?</instructions>

choices.text: When Lisa parked her scooter next to Mr. Pruitt's car, she noticed that the scooter had a flat tire.
When Lisa parked her scooter next to Mr. Pruitt's car, she noticed that it had a flat tire.

header.text: When writing, make sure to avoid vague pronoun references. A vague pronoun reference occurs when a pronoun could refer to more than one possible antecedent.

sentences.text: When Lisa and Kim finally landed, she breathed a sigh of relief.
The pronoun she could refer to either Lisa or Kim, so the meaning of the sentence is unclear.

header.text: Vague pronoun references can be corrected in one of two ways:

sentences.text: 1. Replace the pronoun with its correct antecedent:
When Lisa and Kim finally landed, Lisa breathed a sigh of relief.
2. Rewrite the sentence:
Lisa breathed a sigh of relief when she and Kim finally landed.

header.text: A vague pronoun reference also occurs when they, them, their, theirs, it, or its is used without its antecedent.

sentences.text: They say that this nail polish dries in less than five minutes.
The pronoun they is used without its antecedent, so the meaning of the sentence is unclear.

header.text: This problem can be fixed by replacing the pronoun with its missing antecedent.

contents.text: The advertisements say that this nail polish dries in less than five minutes.
